body_en:
This article is reposted from the Douyin creator Yang Xiang Yuncai (Douyin ID: 2241227819).

This is a photograph I've never quite dared to look at twice. Not because I'm soft-hearted — soft-hearted people look and feel pain; I look and feel like a terrible person. Mostly because looking doesn't help, so I don't dare look again. But then I thought: looking once or twice makes no difference to the people in the photograph. The difference is in me. So I pulled it up and stared at it for a long time.

The photo was taken by Lu Guang in Shangcai, Henan, at the end of 2001. In those years, the place had a name in the news: the “AIDS village.”

The story starts in the 1990s. Back then, people came to the villages to buy blood: a little blood drawn, cash in hand. The farmers did the math and figured it was like carrying water from the river — the water comes from your own body, it grows back after you draw it out, but a few dozen yuan is a few dozen yuan, enough to buy the kid a new pair of shoes, enough for two jin of pork. So they lined up.

I later read some accounts of how the blood stations operated. The blood was drawn out, and a centrifuge separated the plasma — plasma was worth money. What was left was red blood cells. Red cells weren't worth anything, and you can't just throw something away because it's worthless — what a waste. So they mixed the cells with saline and transfused them back into each person's veins. There was a technical problem, though: hundreds of people's red cells mixed together in one bucket, and if just one of them carried the virus, the whole bucket was ruined. No — worse than ruined. That bucket would distribute the virus evenly to every single person, without missing a single one.

In principle, this isn't hard to understand, but nobody thought about it that way at the time. I've thought about it for them: a needle costs a few cents; changing it would cost almost nothing over a year. But the blood station boss didn't think that way. He looked at today — a few extra cents today is a few extra cents. The farmers didn't think that way either. They looked at the here and now — the kid needs school, needs food. Neither side was wrong. But put the two together, and it kills. If you insist on blaming someone, blame the blood station boss: he left one thing out of his calculation — human life. Later the virus joined in too. The virus doesn't recognize money; it only recognizes people.

The photograph is the end of that story. In winter, the wheat seedlings are green, hugging the ground. Two graves sit in the green — the only patches of earth on that land where nothing grows. The graves aren't tall; the soil is dark brown, pressed down with a layer of dry grass, probably to keep the wind from scattering it. No headstone, no cement, no brick. Two black-and-white portraits lean directly against the grass on the graves, one on each side — a man and a woman — and a gust of wind would knock them over. When a person dies and even their photograph has to be propped up by grass, it's not a pleasant thing to say, but that's what's in the photo, and I can't add a headstone for them.

In front of the graves are three oranges, their skins already wrinkled, and two white candles, both lit, their flames small and slightly bent. The candles are freshly lit, which means someone has been here. Who, the photograph doesn't say.

The boy kneels before the grave on the left, ten or so years old, in a grey-green jacket several sizes too big, zippered halfway up, sleeves too long, covering his wrists. The wind lifts the jacket, and it billows emptily against his back. The jacket was probably his father's — that judgment needs no evidence; the size alone is enough.

Yellow paper is burning — no open flame, just pale blue-white smoke. The smoke rises, reaches him, veers slightly, skirts around his face, and drifts up to the right. He doesn't move; his eyes stay open. On this side of the photo, I instinctively turned my head away, though no smoke was blowing into his face in the picture. I turned anyway. Sometimes people flinch from things that aren't there, which probably means some things are real.

Ash drifts up and lands on the bridge of his nose, and he doesn't wipe it off. He sits there like a stone.

This smoke is burned for the dead. The dead rot in the ground; the living choke in the smoke. It sounds neat as a sentence, but that's how it is. If they didn't burn it, all that would be left before the graves is two mounds of dirt.

His hands are pressed together against his chest, in a very proper posture, as if someone taught him, as if he practiced. Who is he praying to? I don't know that. The parents in front of him have become ghosts; the heavens above say nothing. Deaf heaven, mute earth — that's roughly what it means. Those four words are too neat, so neat I hardly dare believe them. If he really prayed for something, I couldn't hear it anyway, so I won't make it up for him.

By rights, this is a moment for crying. He isn't crying. Maybe he can't cry; maybe he cried long ago. This place is desolate — who would he cry for? And after crying, no one would brush the dust from his shoulders, no one would pay next semester's school fees.

When I was a child, I heard a saying: good is rewarded with good. The advantage of that saying is that it's convenient — push the reward into the future, and you don't have to deal with the present. But looking at things as they are now, I can't see when that reward is supposed to arrive. Some suffering can be endured, and once endured it becomes “experience,” something you can write into a book someday. Some suffering can't be endured, and what can't be endured isn't called experience — it's called suffering for nothing. Poverty means having no money; this place has one more layer on top of having no money — even crying has to be weighed for whether it's useful.

Those three oranges before the graves — I stared at them for a long time. I've always had a problem with the idea of dignity: when city people hold a funeral, they set up a memorial hall, read eulogies, and say the deceased worked diligently all their life and lived frugally. Dignity here is three oranges and two candles, which by ordinary standards doesn't count as dignity. But then I thought: dignity is for the living to see. Three oranges set there are there so that passersby know this family hasn't forgotten. Once forgotten, there really is nothing left. So those three oranges do more than many eulogies.

In those years, the outside world was buzzing — the millennium, the Olympic bid, the bell-ringing on the stock exchange, something on television every day. None of it had anything to do with this child, which is only normal: the things on television have nothing to do with most people. Most people's lives run on a different track, one that never makes it onto television. Farther out in the field there's another grave, the same mound of earth, but with no portrait. Having a portrait means someone still remembers; without one, it's hard to say.

I saved this photograph, in a folder I don't often open. Sometimes, when I think of it, I open it and look, then close it again. I wrote this article, honestly, not for him — because I looked at the photograph and felt uneasy, and writing it out makes me feel a little better. Thinking about it that way, I feel like a terrible person all over again. But I can't do anything else. I can't bring his parents back to life, and I can't pay that semester's school fees for him. All I can do is remember that there was such an event, such a person, kneeling in the winter of 2001 before two graves with no headstones.

Remembering this does him no good. It does me a little good. That's roughly what “meaning” is, although I don't much like the word.
excerpt_en: In the winter of 2001, photographer Lu Guang captured a boy kneeling before his parents' unmarked graves in Shangcai, Henan — the end of a story that began with a blood-selling scandal that spread HIV through entire villages.
title_en: The Land and the Green Smoke of 2001
